profile.feeling: A warming bite: ginger tea in winter, Asian dishes, spice jars.

examples.text: אֲנִי שׁוֹתָה תֵּה עִם זַנְגְּבִיל וְלִימוֹן.
examples.tr: I (f.) drink tea with ginger and lemon.

synonyms.nuance: the English loan (pronounced jínjer), usual on drink menus: תה ג׳ינג׳ר
a rare word from Babylonian Aramaic, known from old texts; never used in the kitchen

etymology.text: Medieval borrowing from Arabic زَنْجَبِيل (zanjabīl), and earlier still from Aramaic זַנְגְּבִילָא (zangḇīlā). Compare the rare Hebrew גִּנְבָּר (ginbār), from Jewish Babylonian Aramaic גִּינְבְּרָא (ginbərā).

funFacts: Arabic زَنْجَبِيل, Turkish zencefil, German Ingwer and English ginger all go back to the same ancient word (Greek ζιγγίβερις, from a South Asian source).
The Quran (76:17) names زَنْجَبِيل as the flavour of a drink in paradise.
pitfalls: Do not confuse the colloquial ג׳ינג׳ר (ginger) with ג׳ינג׳י — that is a redhead (also from English “ginger”, the hair colour).
A mass noun: “some ginger” is just זַנְגְּבִיל; there is no everyday plural.
subtleties: On spice jars and in recipes the word is זַנְגְּבִיל; on café menus (ginger tea, ginger beer) the English loan ג׳ינג׳ר is very common.

senses.def: fennel (the bulb vegetable, its leaves and seeds)

examples.tr: I (f.) add sliced fennel to the salad.
At the market I bought fennel and tomatoes.
This fennel is very fresh.
Fennel tea is good for the stomach.

synonyms.nuance: the old native word, largely displaced by שֻׁמָּר (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Akkadian 𒌑𒄩 (šimru, “fennel”). See Arabic شَمَر (šamar, “fennel”) for other cognates. Largely displaced the native Hebrew synonym גּוּפְנָן (gup̄nān, “fennel”).

funFacts: Arabic شَمَر (šamar) is the same word, and Hebrew שָׁמִיר “dill” comes from the same Akkadian source (Wiktionary, Arabic شمر).
Greek μάραθο(ν) “fennel” gave its name to Marathon — the “fennel field”.
pitfalls: The everyday spelling שומר is the same as שׁוֹמֵר “guard; keeps” — only the vowels or the context tell them apart.
The vowel is u: shu-MAR (kubutz, and a dagesh in the מ).
subtleties: The same word names the bulb, the feathery leaves and the seeds (זַרְעֵי שֻׁמָּר) used as a spice.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. The international word goes back (Wiktionary, English asparagus) to Medieval Latin asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

funFacts: German Spargel and Greek σπαράγγι come from the same Greek word; Turkish calls it kuşkonmaz, “the bird does not land”.
pitfalls: No plural in everyday use: “I bought asparagus” is קָנִיתִי אַסְפָּרָגוֹס; single spears are גִּבְעוֹלֵי אַסְפָּרָגוֹס.
subtleties: White asparagus is the same plant, grown covered with soil so that it never sees light.

profile.feeling: A starchy, slightly slimy corm from Egyptian and other Middle Eastern home cooking.

senses.def: taro (the edible corm of Colocasia esculenta)

examples.tr: She cooks taro with chard.
Taro has to be peeled with gloves.

examples.text: אַף פַּעַם לֹא אוֹכְלִים קוֹלְקָס חַי.
examples.tr: Taro is never eaten raw.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; some recipes use the English/Polynesian name “taro” in Hebrew letters.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. Its Arabic entry قُلْقَاس (qulqās, “taro”) derives the word from Classical Syriac ܩܠܩܐܣ (qōlqās) and cites Mishnaic Hebrew קולקס, קרקס (“taro”) from the same source.

funFacts: Arabic قُلْقَاس (qulqās) is the same word; in some Aramaic dialects it once meant a kind of cardoon or artichoke (Wiktionary).
The botanical genus Colocasia and the Cypriot Greek κολοκάσι (a Cypriot speciality) are the same ancient word.
pitfalls: Raw taro contains needle-like crystals (calcium oxalate) that irritate the mouth and the skin: it is always cooked, and peeled with gloves.
subtleties: A rare word for most Israelis; it lives on in families from Egypt and neighbouring countries and in botany books.

profile.feeling: A yellow weed of lawns and fields; bitter leaves for foragers; a wish blown into the wind.

senses.def: dandelion (the plant; its leaves are eaten as a bitter green)

examples.tr: In spring there are dandelions all over the field.
She adds dandelion leaves to the salad.

examples.text: הַיֶּלֶד נוֹשֵׁף עַל שִׁינָן וּמְבַקֵּשׁ מִשְׁאָלָה.
examples.tr: The child blows on a dandelion and makes a wish.

profile.synonymsNone: No true synonym: סַבְיוֹן and מַרְגָּנִית, sometimes given as translations, are other wild plants (groundsel and pimpernel).

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no entry for the noun (the page שינן holds only the verb שִׁנֵּן); its English entry dandelion gives שינן (šinán, m.). English dandelion is from Old French dent de lion, “lion’s tooth”.

funFacts: Most European names mean “lion’s tooth”: French dent-de-lion, German Löwenzahn, English dandelion (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Same letters as the verb שִׁנֵּן “to memorize” (past tense שינן) — without vowels only the context separates them.
subtleties: As food, Hebrew usually says עֲלֵי שִׁינָן (dandelion leaves); שִׁינָן alone is the plant.

examples.tr: He likes pickled turnip.

examples.text: אֲנִי מְבַשֶּׁלֶת מָרָק עִם לְפָתוֹת וּבָצָל.
examples.tr: I (f.) cook a soup with turnips and onion.
At the market the turnips are cheap today.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *lapt-. Cognate with Arabic لِفْت (lift), Classical Syriac ܠܰܦܬܳܐ (laftā) and Akkadian laptu, all “turnip” (Wiktionary, Arabic لفت).

funFacts: One of the oldest Semitic vegetable words: Arabic لِفْت, Syriac ܠܰܦܬܳܐ and Akkadian laptu are the same word.
The pink pickled turnips of Middle Eastern restaurants get their colour from a slice of beetroot (סֶלֶק) in the jar.
pitfalls: Feminine: לֶפֶת כְּבוּשָׁה, not *כָּבוּשׁ; plural לְפָתוֹת.
subtleties: Arabic لِفْت also covers kale and rutabaga (Wiktionary); Hebrew לֶפֶת is the turnip, and the swede has no everyday Hebrew name.

profile.feeling: Bitter wild leaves picked in winter; a bitter herb of the Seder.

senses.def: chicory, endive (Cichorium; bitter leaves, also the pale Belgian-endive heads)

examples.tr: In winter people gather chicory in the fields.

examples.text: הוּא מְטַגֵּן עֲלֵי עֹלֶשׁ עִם בָּצָל.
examples.tr: He fries chicory leaves with onion.

examples.text: יֵשׁ מִשְׁפָּחוֹת שֶׁאוֹכְלוֹת עֹלֶשׁ בְּלֵיל הַסֵּדֶר.
examples.tr: Some families eat chicory on Seder night.

synonyms.nuance: the French loan used in shops for the pale, tight Belgian-endive heads

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. The word is old: the Mishnah (Pesachim 2:6) already lists עֻלְשִׁין among the bitter herbs of Passover.

funFacts: The Mishnah (Pesachim 2:6) lists עֻלְשִׁין among the vegetables that can serve as the bitter herb at the Seder, next to חֲזֶרֶת.
English endive goes back, via Byzantine Greek ἔντυβον and Latin intibus, to Aramaic הִנְדְּבָא — also the source of Arabic هِنْدِبَاء (hindibāʔ) (Wiktionary).
Roasted chicory root was a classic coffee substitute (German Zichorienkaffee).
pitfalls: Article with qamats before ע: הָעֹלֶשׁ.
Everyday spelling with ו: עולש.
subtleties: Hebrew does not separate the two Cichorium salads: עֹלֶשׁ is chicory and endive alike (Wiktionary: “chicory, endive”).

examples.tr: She makes a purslane salad with lemon.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. Compare Arabic رِجْلَة (rijla), an alternative form of رِجْل (rijl), “common purslane” (Wiktionary, Arabic entry).

funFacts: Greek calls it γλιστρίδα and Turkish semizotu (“fat herb”); in Arabic it is رِجْلَة, the same word as Hebrew.
Purslane is one of the richest leafy sources of plant omega-3 fatty acids.
pitfalls: Same letters as רַגְלָהּ “her leg” (רגלה); only the vowels and the context separate them.
subtleties: The article takes qamats before ר: הָרְגֵלָה.
Feminine: רְגֵלָה טְרִיָּה (fresh purslane).

senses.def: Jerusalem artichoke, sunchoke (tuber of Helianthus tuberosus)

examples.tr: I (m.) cook Jerusalem artichoke soup.

examples.text: הָאַרְטִישׁוֹק הַיְּרוּשַׁלְמִי גָּדֵל מַהֵר מְאוֹד בַּגִּנָּה.

etymology.text: אַרְטִישׁוֹק “artichoke” (ultimately from Italian articiocco … from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف, al-ḵuršūf; probably entered Hebrew through Russian and Yiddish) + יְרוּשַׁלְמִי “of Jerusalem” (ירושלים + ־י).

funFacts: The Hebrew name copies English “Jerusalem artichoke”, whose “Jerusalem” is popularly explained as a corruption of Italian girasole, “sunflower”.
Other languages: German and Russian Topinambur / топинамбур, Turkish yer elması (“earth apple”).
pitfalls: It is not an artichoke and not from Jerusalem: it is the tuber of a sunflower (Helianthus tuberosus).
The adjective agrees and takes the article too: הָאַרְטִישׁוֹק הַיְּרוּשַׁלְמִי.
subtleties: On its own, יְרוּשַׁלְמִי means “a Jerusalemite”, and הַיְּרוּשַׁלְמִי can mean the Jerusalem Talmud; in the kitchen the phrase is fixed.

profile.feeling: A stinging weed — painful to touch, good to eat once cooked.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. The word is Biblical: it occurs once, in Isaiah 55:13 (הַסִּרְפַּד), and Modern Hebrew gave it to the nettle. Arabic uses another word, قُرَّاص (qurrāṣ, “nettle”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Isaiah 55:13 promises that the myrtle will come up instead of the nettle — the only time סִרְפַּד appears in the Bible.
Turkish ısırgan (“the biting one”) and German Brennnessel (“burning nettle”) describe the sting; Greek says τσουκνίδα.
pitfalls: The plant stings only raw: cooking or drying removes the sting.
Masculine: סִרְפָּד צָעִיר (young nettle).
subtleties: Mostly used without a plural for the plant as food: מְרַק סִרְפָּד, תֵּה סִרְפָּד.

profile.feeling: A pale, sweet, slightly spicy cousin of the carrot in winter soups.

examples.text: אֲנִי מוֹסִיפָה גֶּזֶר לָבָן לִמְרַק הָעוֹף.
examples.tr: I (f.) add parsnip to the chicken soup.

examples.tr: Parsnips roasted in the oven are very sweet.
At the market he is looking for parsnip.

etymology.text: גֶּזֶר “carrot” + לָבָן “white” (from Proto-West Semitic *laban-; cognate with Arabic لَبَن, laban, “milk”). English parsnip is from Latin pastināca (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew לָבָן “white” and Arabic لَبَن (laban) “milk” are the same Semitic word (Wiktionary).
Latin pastināca also gave German Pastinake and Greek παστινάκη.
pitfalls: Both words agree and both take the article: הַגֶּזֶר הַלָּבָן, הַגְּזָרִים הַלְּבָנִים.
Do not mix it up with שֹׁרֶשׁ פֶּטְרוֹזִילְיָה (parsley root), which looks similar but is smaller and tastes of parsley.
subtleties: Literally “white carrot”: Hebrew names the parsnip after its closest everyday relative.

funFacts: Many languages name the plant after its taste: English sorrel (from Old French sur “sour”), German Sauerampfer, Arabic حُمَّاض (from “sour”).
pitfalls: Everyday spelling with ו: חומעה.
Feminine: חֻמְעָה טְרִיָּה.
subtleties: The sourness comes from oxalic acid, so sorrel is eaten in moderation.

profile.feeling: Pungent red or white relish next to gefilte fish; the bitter herb of Passover.

senses.def: horseradish (the root and the grated relish)
one of the bitter herbs (maror) of the Passover Seder

examples.text: סַבְתָּא מַגִּישָׁה דָּג מְמֻלָּא עִם חֲזֶרֶת אֲדֻמָּה.
examples.tr: Grandma serves gefilte fish with red horseradish.
This horseradish is very hot!
On Seder night horseradish is eaten as the bitter herb.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in standard Hebrew; some Ashkenazi families still use the Yiddish name for the red relish.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. The word is Mishnaic: חֲזֶרֶת heads the list of Passover bitter herbs in Mishnah Pesachim 2:6.

funFacts: In the Mishnah, חֲזֶרֶת was most likely lettuce — the Talmud (Pesachim 39a) equates it with Aramaic חַסָּא; Ashkenazi Jews came to use horseradish, and Modern Hebrew gave the name to it.
Russian хрен, Yiddish כריין (khreyn) and Ashkenazi kitchens share one Slavic word for it; German says Meerrettich.
pitfalls: Feminine: חֲזֶרֶת חֲרִיפָה.
Without vowels חזרת also spells חֲזָרַת, the construct form of חֲזָרָה “return; rehearsal” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: In shops it is sold ready-grated: red (with beetroot) or white.

profile.feeling: Peppery leaves from cool, clear streams.

examples.tr: Watercress grows in flowing water.
He adds watercress to the sandwich.
I bought watercress for the salad.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; plain גַּרְגִּיר means arugula.

etymology.text: גַּרְגִּיר (here “rocket, cress”) + הַנְּחָלִים “of the streams” (plural of נַחַל “stream, wadi”): “stream rocket”. Arabic جِرْجِير (jirjīr) covers both arugula and watercress and is borrowed from Aramaic גַּרְגִּירָא (“rocket”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English watercress, German Brunnenkresse (“well cress”) and Hebrew “stream rocket” all name the plant after the water it grows in.
pitfalls: Already definite: say אֶת גַּרְגִּיר הַנְּחָלִים, never *הַגַּרְגִּיר הַנְּחָלִים.
Without הַנְּחָלִים, גַּרְגִּיר is arugula — a different plant.
subtleties: נַחַל is a stream or a wadi; Israeli hiking trails are named after נְחָלִים.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. It is בָּצָל “onion” in the reduplicated diminutive pattern (compare כְּלַבְלַב “puppy” from כֶּלֶב): “little onion”. English shallot is from French échalote, from Latin ascalonia (cēpa), “onion of Ashkelon” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The European name remembers a city in Israel: Latin ascalonia “of Ashkelon” → French échalote → English shallot — and also English scallion (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The plural doubles the ל: בְּצַלְצַלִּים.
Not the same as בָּצָל יָרֹק (spring onion).
subtleties: The repeated צַל is a diminutive, as in כְּלַבְלַב “puppy” and חֲתַלְתּוּל “kitten”.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From German Mangold (Wiktionary: from Middle High German man(e)golt; further origin unknown).

funFacts: Chard is the same species as beetroot (Beta vulgaris), bred for its leaves instead of its root — hence the botanical name סֶלֶק עָלִים, “leaf beet”.
Turkish calls it pazı and Greek σέσκουλο.
pitfalls: A mass noun: מַנְגּוֹלְד טָרִי, no plural in everyday use; the leaves are עֲלֵי מַנְגּוֹלְד.
subtleties: Hebrew took the German name; English says (Swiss) chard. Seed packets may add the botanical סֶלֶק עָלִים.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. The plant name matches Arabic جِرْجِير (jirjīr, “arugula; watercress”), which Wiktionary derives from Aramaic גַּרְגִּירָא (gargīrā, “rocket”), from Akkadian girgirû.

funFacts: Arabic جِرْجِير (jirjīr) is the same word, from Aramaic and ultimately Akkadian (Wiktionary).
English rocket and arugula and Italian rucola come from Latin ērūca (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: גַּרְגִּיר also means “a grain, a granule” (גַּרְגִּיר אֹרֶז, גַּרְגִּיר חוֹל); the context decides.
As a salad green it is a mass noun: “some arugula” is just גַּרְגִּיר.
subtleties: גַּרְגִּיר הַנְּחָלִים (“stream rocket”) is watercress — a different plant.

Everyday spelling with double י: מלוחייה.
subtleties: The plant is jute mallow (Corchorus olitorius) — the same genus that gives jute fibre.

synonyms.nuance: on its own סֶלֶרִי can mean the root or the stalks; adding שֹׁרֶשׁ makes clear that the root is meant

etymology.text: שֹׁרֶשׁ “root” (from Proto-Semitic *šurš-) + סֶלֶרִי “celery” (an international word; Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry for it). English celeriac is celery + -ac (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Celeriac and celery (כַּרְפַּס) are one species, Apium graveolens: one bred for its root, the other for its stalks.
שֹׁרֶשׁ is also the grammatical “root” of a Hebrew word — and ש־ר־ש is itself a root.
pitfalls: The plural changes the first word: שָׁרְשֵׁי סֶלֶרִי (said shorshei, spelled שורשי).
The article goes on the second word: שֹׁרֶשׁ הַסֶּלֶרִי, not *הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ סֶלֶרִי.
subtleties: In שָׁרְשֵׁי the first vowel is a qamats katan, pronounced o.

funFacts: סָגֹל comes from סֶגֶל “violet (the flower)”, while the vowel sign סֶגוֹל comes from Aramaic סְגוֹלָא “cluster” (Wiktionary).
Turkish can also say mor soğan, “purple onion”, just like Hebrew.
pitfalls: Both words agree and take the article: הַבָּצָל הַסָּגֹל, הַבְּצָלִים הַסְּגֻלִּים.
Everyday spelling with ו: בצל סגול, בצלים סגולים.
subtleties: Hebrew says “purple” (סָגֹל) where English says “red”; בָּצָל לָבָן (white onion) and בָּצָל יָרֹק (spring onion) follow the same noun + colour pattern.
